outcome: The two-dimensional question was answered in 2023, before the window: the hat (arXiv 20 Mar 2023) gives a monotile whose tilings need mirror images, and the spectre (arXiv 28 May 2023) gives a monotile that tiles only aperiodically even with reflections forbidden. No event since 26 Jan 2024 settles or moves the 2D question. Window activity is 2D re-proofs and expositions, plus a 16 Sep 2026 sole-author preprint (Tsiokos, 'Chair44') claiming a strongly aperiodic monotile in three dimensions, found with an AI model; that answers the 3D analogue, not this bullet.
problem_asks: (1) Does there exist a single two-dimensional shape that is the prototile of a tiling of the plane; (2) must that shape admit at least one aperiodic (non-periodic) tiling of the plane; (3) must that same shape admit no periodic tiling of the plane. The statement does not say whether mirror-image tiles are allowed, what matching rules are permitted, or which notion of aperiodic applies. It does not ask for strong aperiodicity (no infinite cyclic symmetry). Read with reflections allowed, the answer is yes by the hat (event hat-2023-03). Read with reflections forbidden, the answer is yes by the spectre (event spectre-2023-05).

events.what_happened: David Smith, Joseph Samuel Myers, Craig S. Kaplan and Chaim Goodman-Strauss post 'An aperiodic monotile' (arXiv:2303.10798). They introduce the hat, a 13-sided polykite made of eight kites, and a continuum of related polygons. The abstract says the shape 'admits tilings of the plane, but never periodic tilings'. Metatile clusters with substitution rules force hierarchical, hence aperiodic, tilings. The case analysis behind the hierarchy is computer-assisted (Python code, cross-checked by two independent implementations per the paper's Section 1.2 as extracted). The paper is listed as published in Combinatorial Theory in June 2024, volume 4, issue 1 (per Kaplan's project page; the journal header itself could not be opened).
events.revisions: v1 20 Mar 2023; v2 29 May 2023; v3 3 Jul 2024 (after journal publication). Journal publication June 2024 per Kaplan's page (secondary).
events.delivers: Under the reflection-permitted reading: a single polygon (the hat, and its continuum family) whose tilings of the plane are all aperiodic. So it is a prototile admitting aperiodic tilings and no periodic tiling, which is the full question as worded with mirror images allowed. The paper and Kaplan's page state the hat's tilings need mirror-image tiles (Waterloo news quotes the first paper: 'as the shape required reflection to tile aperiodically').
events.remains: Under a reflection-free reading (tiles only translated and rotated), the hat does not qualify, because its tilings need mirror images. That reading is addressed by spectre-2023-05. Nothing else in problem_asks remains open for this event.

checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed mathematics journal; editors and referees not named in what I could open
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper (vol. 4, iss. 1, June 2024 per Kaplan's project page). Referee reports not public.

checked_by.qualification: Authors of published work on aperiodic tilings (Discrete & Computational Geometry, per arXiv comment)
checked_by.what_they_did: Gave an independent alternative proof that the monotile of Smith et al. is aperiodic, for one member of the family (see akiyama-araki-2023-07). This is a re-proof of the family, not a check of the hat's own write-up.

events.directly_checkable: The hat polykite and its tile patches can be drawn and checked by hand. Kaplan's project page links an interactive hat patch builder, an H7/H8 substitution app, and a Python re-implementation of the computer-assisted analysis (validate.tar.gz) under a BSD 3-clause licence.
events.direction: Affirmative: produces a single tile whose tilings are aperiodic-only, the answer yes to the question as worded with reflections allowed.
events.object: The hat: a polykite made of eight 60-90-120-90 kites from the Laves tiling, forming a 13-sided figure. Its prototile set is the hat together with its mirror image. Explicit construction: metatile clusters with substitution rules generate tilings of the plane; non-periodicity follows from a combinatorial argument with a computer-assisted case analysis. The construction extends to a continuous family in the edge parameters.

events.what_happened: Smith, Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss post 'A chiral aperiodic monotile' (arXiv:2305.17743). They modify the edges of the hat family to get Spectres, which are strictly chiral aperiodic monotiles: they tile the plane only non-periodically using translations and rotations alone, even when reflections are permitted. The equilateral member, Tile(1,1), is weakly chiral: aperiodic only if reflections are forbidden. Journal: Combinatorial Theory 4(2) (2024), DOI 10.5070/C64264241 (per arXiv journal-ref field).
events.revisions: v1 28 May 2023; v2 28 Sep 2024 (journal version era; no new claim identified).
events.delivers: Under the reflection-forbidden reading: a single polygon (the Spectre) tiling the plane only aperiodically with translations and rotations alone. Under the reflection-permitted reading it also qualifies. Together with hat-2023-03, this covers every part of problem_asks under both readings.
events.remains: Nothing of the 2D question. Strong aperiodicity (no infinite cyclic symmetry, a stricter notion the bullet does not use) is not addressed by this paper.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, vol. 4, iss. 2 (2024), per arXiv journal-ref. Referee reports not public.

events.directly_checkable: The Spectre tile and its substitution tiling can be drawn by hand from the paper; Kaplan's project page provides an interactive tool for Tile(1,1) patches and SVG outlines of Spectre variants.
events.direction: Affirmative under the strict (reflection-forbidden) reading; the answer is yes without any mirror-image caveat.
events.object: The Spectre: a polygon obtained from the hat family by modifying edge lengths. Its tilings follow a hierarchical substitution system. The shape is given explicitly in the paper. Non-periodicity is established by a combinatorial argument with a computer-assisted case analysis (the paper's Section 4, as extracted).

events.what_happened: Shigeki Akiyama and Yoshiaki Araki post 'An alternative proof for an aperiodic monotile' (arXiv:2307.12322). A search excerpt identifies the tile as the Turtle, one family member. They use a Golden Hex substitution with an explicit transition diagram and a 'Golden Ammann bar' linear marking. Versions after v1 revise the paper; it is listed as 'to appear in Discrete and Computational Geometry'.

events.remains: Nothing in problem_asks. The result is restricted to one family member and is a re-proof of non-periodicity.

events.what_happened: James Smith posts 'Turtles, Hats and Spectres: Aperiodic structures on a Rhombic tiling' (arXiv:2403.01911). He derives the monotiles from rhombus tiles with matching rules, treating the tiling as a colouring game on a Rhombille tiling. He gives a recursive substitution system proving non-periodicity 'without computer-aided verification', a Fibonacci-word route to non-periodicity, a deformation of the Turtle into the Hat giving a third non-periodicity proof, and two new substitution rules for Spectre tilings.
events.revisions: v1 only (4 Mar 2024).
events.delivers: Alternative non-periodicity proofs for the Turtle and for the Hat, and new substitution rules for the Spectre. All are restricted to hat-family tiles already settled in 2023. No new existence statement.
events.remains: Nothing in problem_asks.
events.directly_checkable: The substitution rules and the deformation argument can be checked by hand from the paper.
events.direction: Affirmative (non-periodicity restated by new proofs). No change in direction.

events.delivers: A group-tiling analogue: an aperiodic group monotile obtained from the hat under the framework's additional conditions. It says nothing new about tilings of the Euclidean plane.
events.remains: The Euclidean-plane bullet is untouched; that question was already settled in 2023.
events.direction: Analogue in group tilings: affirmative in that setting. Not a direction on the Euclidean-plane bullet.

events.what_happened: Ioannis Tsiokos (Athens; Automorph Inc.) posts 'A Strongly Aperiodic Monotile in Three Dimensions' (arXiv:2609.19214). He claims a single rational polyhedral 3-ball, called Chair44 (R44): a seven-cube chair (a 2×2×2 block with one corner block removed) with 24 exposed unit faces carrying small square-pyramid features. He claims every tiling of R^3 by congruent copies, reflections allowed, has no translational period and a symmetry group of order at most 24, and is homochiral with a nested supertile hierarchy. The proof combines written geometric lemmas with exhaustive finite enumerations, which the abstract says are kernel-checked in Lean 4 'modulo the named compiler hooks' (native_decide). The paper's 'Use of AI systems' disclosure (extraction) says the solid was found by an AI reasoning model and that automated coding agents implemented code, and that text was largely written by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic). Quanta (23 Sep 2026) quotes Tsiokos: 'The 3D Einstein was found by Astra, not me.'
events.revisions: The arXiv abstract page lists v1 only (16 Sep 2026, 12:15 UTC). The HTML copy's title block reads 'revision 2' (baseline commit d90313a717). The v2 URL returned 404. Unresolved.
events.delivers: 3D only: asserts a strongly aperiodic monotile in R^3 (every tiling non-periodic, finite symmetry group, reflections allowed). This answers the analogous 3D question in the affirmative. It does not touch the 2D bullet.
events.remains: For the 2D bullet, everything remains: the paper is about R^3 and says nothing about the plane.

checked_by.what_they_did: Posted arXiv:2609.24779 (21 Sep 2026), a shorter presentation of the Chair44 construction. He praises the discovery and criticises the original's length and organisation. Per Quanta he spent the time to explain the argument.

Posted arXiv:2609.23783 (20 Sep 2026; v2 29 Sep 2026 corrects a figure), giving matching rules for the same tile class. The author's own press release says Flicker reproduced the finite enumerations and confirmed the Lean code reports success; that is the author's claim, not checked against Flicker's paper.
Reports a finite certificate for the 3D construction (N=3) that reproduces the Chair44 statistics, and says N=4 remains open.

machine_checked.url: Not located. The paper says its repository is in Appendix A, which was not visible; the press release links a public repository, not opened.

events.directly_checkable: The polyhedron (seven-cube chair, 24 exposed faces with bumps) and its matching rules can be drawn and checked by hand on patches. The finite enumerations are machine-run; Flicker and Goodman-Strauss restate the rules and the press release says a second implementation replays them, but I did not verify this.
events.doubts: (1) Single author; not peer reviewed (the author's own press release says the framework has not been peer reviewed). (2) The machine check is 'kernel-checked modulo the named compiler hooks'; native_decide adds the Lean compiler to the trusted base. (3) Goodman-Strauss calls the original needlessly long, with 'irrelevant puff', and says the formal repository is 'not in normal form' and the paper is hard to check. This is a signal about checkability, not a verdict. (4) The author's own disclosure says the text was largely written by an AI system. (5) Version discrepancy: abstract page v1 only, HTML 'revision 2', v2 404. (6) The AI model's name differs across sources (see ai).
events.direction: Affirmative in 3D: a single tile of R^3 whose tilings are all non-periodic, so a yes answer to the 3D analogue. It cuts the 3D analogue in the 'yes' direction and leaves the 2D bullet untouched.
events.object: Chair44 (R44): a closed rational polyhedral 3-ball, a seven-cube chair with 24 exposed unit faces carrying small square-pyramid features. The claim: every tiling of R^3 by congruent copies, reflections allowed, has no translational period and a symmetry group of order at most 24; every tiling is homochiral and contains a unique infinite hierarchy of nested supertiles. The tile is explicit. Non-periodicity rests on written geometric lemmas plus exhaustive finite enumerations, checked by machine per the author.

disputes.summary: Credit for the 3D Chair44 tile. The author says the solid was found by the AI model ('Astra found a 3D einstein using SBT'; 'Astra produced the solid'), and says he only understood the intuitive geometric argument. Goodman-Strauss credits Tsiokos's human inquiry and framework, and attributes the paper's style to LLM-driven writing. Both are recorded; I did not choose between them.

Model name. Quanta calls the model 'GPT-6 Astra'; the author's arXiv text (extracted) says 'OpenAI reasoning model (ChatGPT, Astra)'; the press release and Goodman-Strauss's note say 'ChatGPT Astra'. The record uses the author's string.

summary: The two-dimensional question was settled in 2023 by one family of papers from Smith, Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss. The hat (arXiv:2303.10798, first posted 20 Mar 2023) gives a continuum of monotiles whose tilings need mirror images. The spectre (arXiv:2305.17743, 28 May 2023) gives monotiles that are aperiodic even with reflections forbidden. Both predate the window and are recorded as events. Nothing I found since 26 Jan 2024 changes the 2D answer. Window items on the 2D question are re-proofs or expositions of hat, turtle and spectre non-periodicity (James Smith, arXiv:2403.01911, 4 Mar 2024; Akiyama and Araki, first posted 23 Jul 2023 with revisions through Jan 2025), analogues in group tilings (Coulbois et al., 2024), and spectre symmetry, diffraction and inflation papers. The one new existence claim is Tsiokos's sole-author preprint (arXiv:2609.19214, 16 Sep 2026) for a strongly aperiodic monotile in three dimensions. That answers the 3D analogue, not this bullet. Its author credits an OpenAI model ('ChatGPT Astra') with finding the solid and lists OpenAI Codex as implementing code; the disclosure also says Claude Fable 5.1 largely wrote the text, which I recorded here rather than as a system, because it is exposition. The 2D AI search found nothing: the 2023 papers name no system, and the 2024 'Claude 3' and 'Bing Copilot' paper (arXiv:2405.14379) concerns tilings of the plane by seven rectilinear 24-gons, not aperiodic tiles, so it is recorded as a discounted event. Close calls: (a) Reading of the bullet. With reflections allowed, the hat (2023-03-20) carries the answer. With reflections forbidden, only the spectre (2023-05-28) does. Both are recorded, so the later pass can choose. (b) Sharma's arXiv:2403.09640: the page's v1 line reads 13 Aug 2023, but the 2403 identifier implies March 2024. I could not resolve this, so the date is recorded as 2023-08-13 with predates_frozen_revision null. Its abstract calls its support 'compelling evidence' from simulations, and no engagement was found, so the date only changes the window count. (c) Chair44. It concerns R^3, not the plane. It is not peer reviewed. Its machine check uses native_decide and is 'kernel-checked modulo the named compiler hooks'. Two companion 3D preprints (Flicker; Goodman-Strauss) and a higher-dimensional extension (Kamenetsky) followed within three weeks. Several AI quotations in the 3D entries come from WebFetch extraction of the arXiv HTML, because the PDFs were unreadable binary. They should be checked verbatim before anyone relies on them.
competing_reading: A reader who takes the Einstein problem in the 3D sense of the 2026 papers, a single tile whose tilings are all non-periodic, would count Chair44 as the live answer. That reading moves the 3D analogue, not this 2D bullet. A reader who insists on strong aperiodicity (no infinite cyclic symmetry, Goodman-Strauss's notion) would count the 2D question as still open. I found no 2D result on that notion, and the bullet does not ask for it. I did not check whether the hat or spectre tilings have an infinite cyclic symmetry, and that check would settle the strong-aperiodicity reading.
what_would_settle_it: For the 2D bullet, the primary sources are already in hand (arXiv 2303.10798 and 2305.17743). Still needed: (i) the true first-submission date of arXiv:2403.09640, from the arXiv listing or API (13 Aug 2023 or March 2024); (ii) the Combinatorial Theory header dates for both 2D papers, which the journal site did not return; (iii) verbatim checks of the Tsiokos PDF's 'Use of AI systems' passage and of the Goodman-Strauss note's AI sentences, since both were read through extraction; (iv) confirmation of whether the hat or spectre tilings have an infinite cyclic symmetry, for the strong-aperiodicity reading. None of my searches found a 2D result after 2023 that asserts a reflection-free or strongly aperiodic monotile.

judgement.why: The statement asks for a 2D shape that tiles only aperiodically. It does not forbid reflections or require strong aperiodicity, so the hat (March 2023) answers it in full, and the spectre (May 2023) answers it even with reflections forbidden. Both appeared in a journal of record, both are explicit witnesses, and both predate the snapshot. Every later 2D item is a re-proof, an exposition, a study of the tilings' properties or a formalisation, so its scope is none. Group-tiling and 3D results (Chair44 and its follow-ups) answer changed questions and are variants. Chair44's model really did produce the tile, so it is marked generated, but only for that 3D variant. Its Codex entry covers implementation code, which is not the mathematics, and so is not credited. Greatrix's Claude 3 suggestion concerns unrelated polygons. It is a variant, and the model only conjectured that the shapes tile while the authors built the tilings, so it gets none.
judgement.doubts: Sharma's date cannot be placed (13 Aug 2023 on the page vs a 2403 identifier), and the Kaplan survey is year-only 2024; neither affects anything. The hat's journal publication date comes from a secondary source.
